The changes would apply to income years starting on 1 July 2026.

Moved the second reading of the Superannuation (Building a Stronger and Fairer Super System) Imposition Bill 2026, which operates with related legislation to support the proposed superannuation reforms, and commended it to the House.

Argued that the Treasury Laws Amendment (Building a Stronger and Fairer Super System) Bill 2026 imposed an unmandated tax and threatened retirement security, while the government said it would better target concessions, strengthen the LISTO and support low-income workers.

Moved to suspend standing and sessional orders so two superannuation bills could be debated in cognate, with variations limited to motions moved by a Minister; a motion to put the question was subsequently moved.

Asked about making superannuation fairer and more sustainable; the Treasurer said the Superannuation (Building a Stronger and Fairer Super System) Imposition Bill 2026 was likely to pass without amendment, increasing support for low-income members while making concessions for larger balances more sustainable.

Opposed the Treasury Laws Amendment (Building a Stronger and Fairer Super System) Bill 2026 and related bill, arguing they imposed a new superannuation tax, weakened certainty and reflected excessive government spending. This bill is part of a package that creates the Australian Tertiary Education Commission as the main oversight body for the higher education system.

The commission would be run by three independent commissioners—including a First Nations commissioner—appointed by the education minister for up to five years, and would negotiate performance agreements with universities.

The bill requires the commission to consider improving outcomes for people facing systemic barriers, such as Indigenous Australians, people with disability, those from low-income backgrounds, and regional residents.
Establishes the Australian Tertiary Education Commission as a steward of higher education.
Creates a National Tertiary Education Objective that the commission must follow.
Requires the commission to negotiate mission-based compacts with higher education providers.
Embeds equity by requiring the commission to improve outcomes for groups facing systemic barriers.
Provides for a First Nations commissioner and a First Nations advisory committee.

Higher education providers, higher education students, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, people with disability, people from low socioeconomic backgrounds, and people in regional Australia.

This bill is part of a package that establishes the Australian Tertiary Education Commission (ATEC) as the steward of the higher education system.
The package would create a National Tertiary Education Objective, require ATEC to consider it, and set up a three-member commission with a First Nations Commissioner.
The package would also introduce mission-based compacts with higher education providers, which could lead to compliance action if not in force for a year.
Establishes the Australian Tertiary Education Commission (ATEC) as the steward of the higher education system.
Creates a National Tertiary Education Objective (NTEO) that ATEC must have regard to.
Provides for ATEC to be led by three independent commissioners, including a First Nations Commissioner.
Requires ATEC to establish a First Nations Advisory Committee.
Introduces mission-based compacts with higher education providers, with potential compliance action under HESA if not in force.
Embeds equity by requiring ATEC to consider improving outcomes for people facing systemic barriers to education.
Higher education providers, students, First Nations communities, and people facing systemic barriers to education.

According to the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd2526/26bd038), which is a document prepared by the parliamentary library: > *The Universities Accord (Australian Tertiary Education Commission) (Consequential and Transitional Provisions) Bill 2025 (the C&T Bill) amends related legislation to implement the Bill, including transferring responsibilities for the Higher Education Standards Framework to [Australian Tertiary Education Commission (ATEC)](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd2526/26bd038), and enabling information sharing between the Department of Education and ATEC.*

Argued that the Universities Accord (Australian Tertiary Education Commission) Bill 2025 and related bill would create another regulator without a clear educational vision, embed inappropriate objectives concerning social development and environmental sustainability, and add to duplication, cost and regulatory complexity, while acknowledging equity and workforce considerations.

Moved to suspend standing and sessional orders, but the Deputy Speaker ruled the proposed motion irrelevant to the bill before the House; then supported bills establishing the Australian Tertiary Education Commission under the Universities Accord, describing its proposed stewardship, equity, funding and provider oversight functions before the debate was interrupted under standing order 43.
Universities Accord (Australian Tertiary Education Commission) (Consequential and Transitional Provisions) Act 2026
The bill would permanently enshrine ASIO's compulsory questioning powers in law instead of letting them expire.

It would expand the types of security threats for which an adult can be questioned under a warrant to include sabotage, communal violence promotion, attacks on defence systems, and serious border integrity threats.
People charged with a related offence that is unresolved or imminent could only be questioned before a retired judge serving as a prescribed authority.
Makes the compulsory questioning framework permanent by removing its sunset provision.
Expands the scope of adult compulsory questioning warrants to cover new security threats defined in the ASIO Act.
Amends rules for the appointment and termination of prescribed authorities to strengthen their independence and impartiality.
Adds a new reporting requirement for conduct under a compulsory questioning warrant.
Introduces a safeguard requiring questioning of a person with an unresolved or imminent related charge to happen only before a retired judge.
ASIO, prescribed authorities, people subject to compulsory questioning warrants, and the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security.

Moved the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation Amendment Bill (No. 2) 2025, which would make ASIO's compulsory questioning powers permanent, expand adult questioning warrants to additional security matters, strengthen safeguards and reporting requirements, and permit a further review three years after commencement; debate was adjourned.

Declared that, unless otherwise ordered, the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation Amendment Bill (No. 2) 2025 stood referred to the Federation Chamber after the second-reading debate was adjourned.

Supported the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation Amendment Bill (No. 2) 2025, arguing that compulsory questioning powers should become permanent, cover additional national security threats and operate with strengthened oversight, reporting and safeguards; noted the powers had been used only 20 times in more than 22 years.

Debated the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation Amendment Bill (No. 2) 2025, which would make compulsory questioning powers permanent, expand eligible matters and strengthen safeguards and oversight; amendments concerning children were proposed, opposition was stated, and the second-reading question remained unresolved.

Moved bills to make ASIO's compulsory questioning powers permanent and broaden their application while strengthening safeguards and oversight, expand National Immunisation Program access to passive immunological products, and make technical social security and veterans' affairs amendments ahead of 1 July 2026.

Argued that compulsory questioning powers remain important for national security but require strong oversight. Supported expanding the matters covered by warrants, subject to retaining a three-year sunset clause; another speaker opposed making the powers permanent, citing concerns about children, legal representation and extraordinary state powers.

Reaffirmed opposition to the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation Amendment Bill (No. 2) 2025, reading constituent objections to its expanded compulsory questioning powers and citing concerns from the Law Council and the Australian Human Rights Commission, while renewing calls for a national human rights act; the government proposed amendments adding a sunset clause and a two-year statutory review of the new powers.

As President, put questions on a series of amendments to the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation Amendment Bill (No. 2) 2025 from the government, the Australian Greens, the United Australia Party, One Nation and Senator David Pocock, covering sunset dates for questioning powers, judicial preference for prescribed authorities, lawyers' rights during ASIO questioning and repeal of minor (under-18) questioning warrants, before the bill passed its remaining stages.

The speaker opposed the Restoring Territory Rights Bill 2022, arguing that territories lack the legislative systems to properly handle euthanasia and that the federal government should address the issue itself rather than devolving power to lower levels of government.

The speaker supported the Dental Benefits Amendment Bill 2021 to remove the minimum age of two for the Child Dental Benefits Schedule, expanding eligibility to all children under 18 and adding around 300,000 children per year at a cost of $5.4 million over four years.
Customs Tariff Amendment (2022 Harmonized System Changes) Bill 2021

The speaker supported the Customs Tariff Amendment Bill to align Australia’s tariff codes with the 2022 international Harmonized System, creating new classifications for drones, 3D printers, edible insects, e-waste, and vaping tobacco, while removing outdated ones like world globes and answering machines. Duty rates for flat panel displays, semiconductor transducers, and e-waste were set to free, and Australia secured preferred classifications for virgin olive oil, placebos in clinical trial kits, LED lighting, and synthetic diamonds.
Customs Tariff Amendment (Incorporation of Proposals) Bill 2021

The speaker argued for amendments to the Customs Tariff Act to extend duty-free imports for COVID-19 medical and hygiene products until 30 June 2021 (reducing receipts by $3.8 million), provide duty-free goods for the F-35A Joint Strike Fighter program (reducing receipts by $6.7 million), and grant duty-free concessions for certain motor vehicles and components used in Australian automotive R&D (reducing receipts by $1.7 million).
Family Law Amendment (A Step Towards a Safer Family Law System) Bill 2020

The speaker argued that the Family Law Amendment (A Step Towards a Safer Family Law System) Bill will protect children by prioritising their wellbeing, and noted that the presumption of equal shared parental responsibility under section 61DA of the Family Law Act does not apply in cases of family violence or abuse. The speaker also announced government investments of $13.5 million for family safety risk screening, $10.4 million for co-located child protection and policing officials in family law courts, and over $48.9 million for family advocacy support services through 2022.
National Consumer Credit Protection Amendment (Supporting Economic Recovery) Bill 2020

The speaker argued that the National Consumer Credit Protection Amendment (Supporting Economic Recovery) Bill 2020 will remove unnecessary barriers to credit for most products while retaining and strengthening responsible lending obligations for high-cost credit, such as small amount credit contracts and consumer leases. They cited the creation of 29,000 new jobs and a 6.4% unemployment rate as signs of economic recovery, and stated the reforms will reduce red tape, improve competition, and introduce new protections including a cap on lessor costs and protected earnings amounts.
Family Assistance Legislation Amendment (Improving Assistance for Vulnerable and Disadvantaged Families) Bill 2020

The speaker supported the Family Assistance Legislation Amendment Bill 2020, which extends additional childcare subsidy periods for children under long-term protection orders and allows backdating up to 13 weeks in exceptional circumstances, as part of the government's transition to a demand-driven childcare subsidy system from 13 July 2020 with $2 billion in subsidies and $708 million in transition payments.
Aged Care Legislation Amendment (Improved Home Care Payment Administration No. 1) Bill 2020

The speaker supported the Aged Care Legislation Amendment (Improved Home Care Payment Administration No. 1) Bill 2020, noting the Morrison government increased the age pension by $117.80 per fortnight for singles and $177.40 for couples in Longman, benefiting 21,433 aged pensioners, with further increases scheduled for March and September each year.
